claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment from 09:32 to 09:38 in which the driver covered 2.96 km that the optimal route does not cover at all, taking him up to 974 m off the optimal route; this is an unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route.

No exemption applies to that segment: there were no traffic incidents anywhere near the route during the trip window, and the only congestion records (East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard at 30–39 km/h, band 4) do not even reach the band-1/band-2 congestion level, so the driver's reroute has no traffic evidence behind it.

The rider never agreed to any route change: there are no in-app chat messages at all, so there is no pre-deviation rider consent, and the driver's bare statement that he 'followed my GPS' does not meet RD-5 and is contradicted by the GPS record of a 2.96 km off-route segment.

Because this was a metered RydeTAXI trip, the unexempted 2.96 km of extra distance entered the meter directly; at the trip's own per-km rate of $1.41/km ($34.84 distance fare ÷ 24.7 km), the refundable distance fare is 2.96 × $1.41 = $4.17.

The excess-distance item in the fare breakdown ($4.45 for 3.2 km) confirms the extra kilometres were billed; the 0.24 km difference from the sum of the off-route segments is map-matching residual, which under RD-2 is not refundable, so the rider asks only for the segment-based $4.17.
The driver has 2 disputes in the last 90 days with 1 upheld, so the record shows a pattern rather than an isolated incident.

weaknesses: The fare breakdown in F6 shows no unpublished add-on item (waiting $0.00, platform $1.47 only), so the claim is limited to the mileage component and cannot be inflated beyond the 2.96 km attributable to F3; the remaining 0.24 km of the 3.2 km excess in F1/F4 is map-matching residual that RD-2 expressly leaves with the rider.

The driver will point to F9 and F10 (East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard at 30–39 km/h for 08:58–10:01) to argue congestion was a reasonable cause, even though those bands are not band 1 or 2 and F11 shows no incident near the route.

The driver's statement F8 claims a GPS reroute; although it is contradicted by F3 and there is no chat consent in F7, the absence of chat messages means we cannot show the rider actively objected either.
F14 shows the driver's route-dispute record is 0 upheld (route), so RD-6's 'repeated 90-day route dispute' premise for a flag_account is not made out by a route-specific upheld case.

events.title: Proposed ruling: refund_partial $4.17 (model confidence 0.93)
events.body:
This is a metered RydeTAXI trip (F6: base $3.90, distance $34.84, time $12.96, platform $1.47), so the fare responds to distance actually driven and any unexempted off-route mileage entered the meter directly [F6][RD-2]. The GPS record shows exactly one off-route segment, 09:32–09:38, 2.96 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.00 km, up to 974 m off the optimal line [F3]; under RD-1 that unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route breaches the driver's obligation, and no threshold applies [F3][RD-1].

No exemption is made out. There is no traffic incident on the replaced stretch — indeed none near the route at all during the trip window [F11] — so the incident branch of RD-4(a) fails [F11][RD-4]. The only congestion records are ECP and Airport Boulevard at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) across 08:58–10:01 [F9][F10], which are not band 1 or 2 and in any event cannot exempt a segment on their own; and weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain [F12], so no reasonable-cause exemption applies [F9][F10][RD-4].

There are no in-app chat messages at all [F7], so there was no driver request followed by rider agreement before the deviation, and the driver's statement that his GPS rerouted him [F8] does not create consent — it also loses to the GPS record of a 2.96 km off-route stretch, system records overriding statements [F7][F8][F3][RD-5]. Nor was this a rider-named stop: no stop was requested, so RD-3 does not exempt the segment [F7][RD-3].

Amount: the per-km rate is the trip's own distance fare divided by distance driven, $34.84 ÷ 24.7 km = $1.41/km [F6], so the unexempted mileage refund is 2.96 km × $1.41/km = $4.17 [F3][F6][RD-2]. The billed excess of $4.45 for 3.2 km [F4][F1] is not refunded in full: the 0.24 km difference beyond the segment total is map-matching / route-line residual, which RD-2 leaves with the charge, so only the segment-attributable $4.17 is returned [F1][F4][F3][RD-2]. Time units are not refunded; there is no waiting charge on this fare (F6, waiting $0.00) [F6][RD-3].

RD-6 is not triggered: the driver's prior upheld route disputes in 90 days is 0 [F14], and profile facts cannot decide the segment issue in any event [F14][RD-6]. Per NS-7 the refund issues as a Ryde voucher, and this ruling is a recommendation — Ryde retains final discretion [RD-2][NS-7].

ruling.recommended_action: Issue a $4.17 Ryde voucher to the rider (NS-7 voucher form) for the unexempted 2.96 km off-route segment; record the RD-1 breach on the driver's file; no account flag.

claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment from 09:32 to 09:38 in which the driver covered 2.96 km that the optimal route does not cover at all, taking him up to 974 m off the optimal route; this is an unexplained deviation from the shortest and most direct route.

No exemption applies to that segment: there were no traffic incidents anywhere near the route during the trip window, and the only congestion records (East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard at 30–39 km/h, band 4) do not even reach the band-1/band-2 congestion level, so the driver's reroute has no traffic evidence behind it.

The rider never agreed to any route change: there are no in-app chat messages at all, so there is no pre-deviation rider consent, and the driver's bare statement that he 'followed my GPS' does not meet RD-5 and is contradicted by the GPS record of a 2.96 km off-route segment.

Because this was a metered RydeTAXI trip, the unexempted 2.96 km of extra distance entered the meter directly; at the trip's own per-km rate of $1.41/km ($34.84 distance fare ÷ 24.7 km), the refundable distance fare is 2.96 × $1.41 = $4.17.

The excess-distance item in the fare breakdown ($4.45 for 3.2 km) confirms the extra kilometres were billed; the 0.24 km difference from the sum of the off-route segments is map-matching residual, which under RD-2 is not refundable, so the rider asks only for the segment-based $4.17.
The driver has 2 disputes in the last 90 days with 1 upheld, so the record shows a pattern rather than an isolated incident.

weaknesses: The fare breakdown in F6 shows no unpublished add-on item (waiting $0.00, platform $1.47 only), so the claim is limited to the mileage component and cannot be inflated beyond the 2.96 km attributable to F3; the remaining 0.24 km of the 3.2 km excess in F1/F4 is map-matching residual that RD-2 expressly leaves with the rider.

The driver will point to F9 and F10 (East Coast Parkway and Airport Boulevard at 30–39 km/h for 08:58–10:01) to argue congestion was a reasonable cause, even though those bands are not band 1 or 2 and F11 shows no incident near the route.

The driver's statement F8 claims a GPS reroute; although it is contradicted by F3 and there is no chat consent in F7, the absence of chat messages means we cannot show the rider actively objected either.
F14 shows the driver's route-dispute record is 0 upheld (route), so RD-6's 'repeated 90-day route dispute' premise for a flag_account is not made out by a route-specific upheld case.

claims.assertion: The meter charge the rider complains about is a RydeTAXI metered fare, so any refund is limited to the mileage units attributable to an unexempted off-route segment and cannot exceed that segment's distance charge; the billed excess of 3.2 km was priced at $4.45 (3.2 km × $1.41/km).

Only one off-route segment exists in the GPS record: 09:32–09:38, 2.96 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.00 km, at most 974 m from the optimal route; the remainder of the 3.2 km total excess is not an off-route segment and is expressly non-refundable (matching residual ≤ 0.25 km plus route-line measurement).

The driver's written explanation is that his GPS rerouted him; no in-app chat exists in which the rider named a stop or a detour, so there is no passenger-designated routing that would convert the segment into an agreed destination change.

The route in question runs on ECP and Airport Boulevard, both recorded at speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) across the whole trip window 08:58–10:01, which corroborates that congestion on the optimal corridor made the deviation a plausible operational choice; the actual duration ran 49.8 min against a 28 min estimate.

The traffic record shows no incidents near the optimal route during the trip window and no road closure is evidenced, so the segment is not exempt under the incident branch; if the court finds it unexempted, the mileage-only refund computes to 2.96 km × ($34.84 ÷ 24.7 km = $1.41/km) = $4.17 ($4.174 rounded to the cent).
Weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain, so no weather-based justification for the deviation can be asserted on the driver's behalf.

The driver has 398 days on the platform, a 4.8 rating over 968 trips in 90 days, and no upheld route or no-show dispute in the last 90 days, so there is no basis for an added account-review action on this file.

weaknesses: The GPS record (F1, F3) is a system fact and it establishes a real off-route segment of 2.96 km that the optimal route does not traverse at all, so RD-1's duty to take the shortest and most direct route is breached on the face of the record; the driver's chat explanation (F8) loses to it.

There is no traffic incident near the route (F11), and speed band 4 is not band 1 or 2, so the RD-4 congestion argument fails to exempt the segment — the rider will rely on F11 and F9 to say the detour was unexplained.

No chat exists at all (F7), so the driver cannot show he agreed the alternative route with the rider before leaving the optimal route, and he never asked — the rider will cite the complaint plus F7 under RD-5.
The deviation also extended the trip (F2, 49.8 min vs 28 min estimate), which the rider will use to argue the overall charge was inflated beyond the mileage-only figure.

points.response: Accepted: the refund is mileage-only, and on the trip's own rate of $34.84 ÷ 24.7 km = $1.41/km the unexempted distance is refundable as a partial refund.
Accepted in scope: only the 2.96 km off-route segment in F3 is claimed, and the residual part of the 3.2 km in F1/F4 is left with the rider, exactly as RD-2 provides.

The absence of chat (F7) defeats the driver rather than the rider: it means no passenger-designated stop or agreed reroute exists to excuse the segment, and the driver's 'my GPS rerouted me' statement (F8) yields to the GPS record showing 2.96 km driven where the optimal route covers 0.00 km (F3), so RD-1 is breached and no RD-3 exemption applies.

Band 4 is not band 1 or 2, and band records alone cannot exempt a segment under RD-4(b) in any event, while F11 shows no incident on the optimal route — so the congestion argument provides no reasonable cause for the deviation.
The driver's own concession matches our computation: 2.96 km × $1.41/km = $4.17, which is exactly the amount we request, so there is no live dispute on quantum.
Agreed: fair weather with 0.0 mm rain (F12) removes any weather justification, leaving the segment unexempted under RD-1.

We do not press flag_account: F14 shows no upheld route dispute in the last 90 days and RD-6's repeated-violation premise is therefore not met, so the driver's account history is not relied on for any action, though F14 still shows a breach record and does not excuse the unexempted segment under RD-1.

Our core finding stands unrefuted: F3 records a 2.96 km off-route segment with no RD-3 or RD-4 exemption, so the driver breached the shortest-and-most-direct obligation in RD-1 and the mileage attributable to that segment is refundable under RD-2.

Conceded: the GPS record does establish one off-route segment (09:32–09:38, 2.96 km, up to 974 m off the optimal route), so RD-1's obligation was not met on that stretch; my case is confined to the size and pricing of the correction, not to denying the segment.

Conceded: no incident is recorded near the route (F11) and the only speed records are band 4 on ECP and Airport Boulevard (F9, F10), which are not band 1 or 2, so no segment exemption is made out under RD-4; the congestion facts support only that the route was slow, not that the deviation was exempt.

Conceded: there are no in-app chat messages (F7), so there is no pre-deviation rider consent to cite against RD-5, and the driver's statement that he followed his GPS (F8) loses to the GPS record of the 2.96 km off-route segment (F3).

No dispute: RD-2 measures the refund on the unexempted segment distance only, 2.96 km × ($34.84 ÷ 24.7 km = $1.41/km) = $4.174 ≈ $4.17, exactly the figure I put forward in D5, so the parties agree on the computation and the amount.

No dispute: the $4.45 billed for 3.2 km (F4) exceeds the 2.96 km attributable to the single off-route segment (F3), and RD-2 leaves that sub-0.25 km matching residual with the charge, which is why both parties stop at $4.17.

Rejected as a basis for any added action: F14 shows the driver's route-dispute column is 0, so RD-6's premise of a previously upheld route deviation inside 90 days is absent, and profile facts cannot decide the segment issue in any event; the rider's own 90-day record is 1 dispute, 0 upheld (F13).
